title: The Empty Fort Strategy: Was Sima Yi Even There? In 228, the One Fooled Was Zhang He
description:
Someone plays a zither on the gate tower and an army of 150,000 below turns and leaves: everyone knows the scene, yet the main text of Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms does not have a word of it.

This episode peels the story back layer by layer, in the order the records were found: the version Guo Chong told early in the Western Jin, in the presence of Sima Jun, Prince of Fufeng (Sima Yi's son) — Yangping, 10,000 against 200,000, flags lowered and drums silenced; no zither, no gate tower, no Sima Zhao, no Jieting. Some 200 years later, Pei Songzhi rebutted it point by point in his notes, opening with "what Guo Chong says is all truly doubtful" and ending with "so we know everything this book says is false". Then come Sima Yi's real months in the Book of Jin: stationed at Wancheng from the 6th month of 227, at the walls of Xincheng in 8 days to strike Meng Da, the city taken in 16 days, back to Wancheng, then a visit to court and orders to hold Wancheng again. In 228 the men who actually faced Zhuge Liang were Cao Zhen and Zhang He, and Emperor Ming of Wei came to Chang'an himself; Sima Yi was not on the list. The day Jieting was lost, Wang Ping's 1,000 men "beat their drums and held firm", so that Zhang He "suspected an ambush and did not press in". In 230 Sima Yi set out from Xicheng (the Xicheng on the upper Han River, not the novel's Xicheng County), cutting through the mountains against Shu, and turned back in heavy rain; only after Cao Zhen died in 231 did he first truly face Zhuge Liang; in 234, after Zhuge Liang's death, the Shu army turned its banners and beat its drums, and he retreated, leaving the saying "a dead Zhuge put a living Zhongda to flight". The zither, the gate tower, Sima Zhao advising his father under the wall, Xicheng and Jieting are all missing from Guo Chong's version; they appear only later, in chapter 95 of the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, and even the poem at the end of that chapter says "later people point at it, doubting to this day".

Quotations from the official histories follow transcriptions of the Wenyuan Pavilion Siku Quanshu edition of the Records of the Three Kingdoms (with Pei Songzhi's notes) and of the Book of Jin; the novel follows Project Gutenberg's 120-chapter edition. The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below; sentences with "I think" or "we think" are the channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

sc001.text: You've heard it: a man plays a zither on the tower; 150,000 troops below turn back.

sc002.text: Jieting just fell. The novel's Zhuge Liang moves grain at Xicheng.

sc003.text: Word comes: Sima Yi is upon them; the town has just 2,500 troops.

sc004.text: He opens the gates; troops sweep as townsfolk;

sc005.text: he sits atop the tower, lights incense, plays.

sc006.text: Sima Yi: Zhuge Liang is cautious. There must be an ambush. Retreat!

sc007.text: Even the novel's Zhuge Liang laughs later: were I Sima Yi, I wouldn't retreat.

sc008.text: But that's not the strangest part. The earliest version was told to Sima Yi's own son.

sc009.text: That year, at the foot of a hill, someone else kept drumming. Who was he fooling?

sc010.text: This file tracks Sima Yi over 7 years in three books.

sc011.text: On the day of the Empty Fort, where was Sima Yi?

sc012.text: To find him, find the earliest form. Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms has not a word in its main text.

sc013.text: The earliest Empty Fort tale hides in later notes on the Records.

sc014.text: It says: decades on, in early Jin, Prince Sima Jun of Fufeng held Guanzhong.

sc015.text: He's the one from the opening: Sima Yi's son.

sc016.text: His officials, discussing Zhuge Liang, mostly mocked him: small strength, big ambitions.

sc017.text: But one guest, a man from Jincheng named Guo Chong, stood up for Zhuge Liang.

sc018.text: He said Zhuge Liang did five things no one knew of.

sc019.text: The Empty Fort was the third.

sc020.text: In that seat, you'd probably say: all right, let's hear it. I would too.

sc021.text: But his version lacks a few things from the scene you know. What's missing?

sc022.text: In Guo Chong's story the place differs: not Xicheng but Yangping, in Hanzhong.

sc023.text: Zhuge Liang sent Wei Yan's army east; just 10,000 held the city.

sc024.text: Sima Yi came with 200,000, just missing Wei Yan, and pushed to within 60 li.

sc025.text: Too late to reach Wei Yan; the officers went pale.

sc026.text: What would Zhuge Liang do now?

sc027.text: He was calm: flags lowered, drums silenced, no one allowed out of the tents.

sc028.text: Then he opened the four gates; streets swept and watered.

sc029.text: If you were a soldier inside, gates wide open, knowing the enemy was near, wouldn't you be nervous?

sc030.text: Sima Yi thought Zhuge Liang always steady; this sudden weakness made him suspicious.

sc031.text: He suspected an ambush, almost the opening's "There must be an ambush."

sc032.text: So he led his army away to the northern hills.

sc033.text: Next day at breakfast Zhuge Liang clapped and laughed to aides:

sc034.text: Sima Yi must think I'm timid, with an ambush; he's gone along the hills.

sc035.text: Scouts came back and reported: exactly so.

sc036.text: Guo Chong said Sima Yi found out later and was vexed.

sc037.text: Honestly, it's a great story. No wonder it survived.

sc038.text: But did Zhuge Liang ever really bluff Sima Yi into retreat?

sc039.text: Notice what's missing? Where's the opening zither?

sc040.text: Guo Chong's version: no zither, no gate tower, no Sima Zhao.

sc042.text: Those only show up in the later novel.

sc043.text: Even the numbers differ. Comparing them the first time, I counted three times.

sc044.text: The novel knows later readers doubted this: the chapter's closing poem ends, "Later people point at it, doubting to this day."

sc045.text: But that year Zhuge Liang really was based around Yangping, as Chen Shou records; Guo Chong didn't pick it out of thin air.

sc046.text: And the Sima Yi standing outside the walls? Was he really there that year?

sc047.text: First to check it seriously: Pei Songzhi, who annotated the Records.

sc048.text: He presented his notes to the emperor in AD 429, about 200 years after that battle.

sc049.text: You'll like his rule: if it doesn't add up, he corrects it at once.

sc050.text: Before Guo Chong's five things he wrote: good stories of Zhuge Liang, I'd love to hear.

sc051.text: But then he wrote: what Guo Chong says is all truly doubtful.

sc052.text: Every time, I laugh: he'd love to hear it, then picks it apart point by point.

sc054.text: As Zhuge Liang reached Yangping, Sima Yi still held Jingzhou, at Wancheng.

sc055.text: He adds: Sima Yi faced Zhuge Liang in Guanzhong only after someone died.

sc057.text: He checked the records again: Wei did send Sima Yi from Wancheng, via Xicheng, against Shu.

sc058.text: Xicheng? Is it the same place as the city in the novel?

sc059.text: Pei Songzhi's point: no fighting at Yangping around then.

sc060.text: The place is off. And the numbers?

sc061.text: Remember Guo Chong's 200,000? So many men, who knew the city had few troops.

sc062.text: Even fearing an ambush, he should camp and go slow. Why turn and leave?

sc063.text: The novel's Zhuge Liang himself said: were I Sima Yi, I wouldn't retreat;

sc064.text: Pei Songzhi worked out exactly the same thing.

sc065.text: See? Two men from different eras, reaching one answer.

sc066.text: Wei Yan, who led the army east? Pei Songzhi checked him too.

sc067.text: Wei Yan always wanted 10,000 men to take another road; Zhuge Liang never agreed.

sc068.text: If he wouldn't give him even that, why hand him the army and keep weak troops himself?

sc069.text: Finally, he looked at who was hearing this story.

sc070.text: Remember the Prince of Fufeng, presiding? The tale shamed his father.

sc071.text: Pei Songzhi: telling a son his father's faults is improper.

sc072.text: Yet the book says the Prince of Fufeng praised it.

sc073.text: So he concluded: everything this book says is false.

sc074.text: That's just Pei Songzhi's word. Do other histories agree on where Sima Yi was that year?

sc075.text: They do. The Book of Jin says that from the 6th month of 227, he was stationed at that same Wancheng.

sc076.text: He led both Jingzhou and Yuzhou.

sc077.text: A year earlier he beat back Wu's Zhuge Jin at Xiangyang.

sc078.text: Year's end: Meng Da of Xincheng revolted.

sc079.text: Meng Da's letter worked it out: Wancheng is 800 li from Luoyang, 1,200 from him.

sc080.text: Doing Meng Da's math, you'd likely feel safe too.

sc082.text: He marched day and night, there in 8 days.

sc083.text: On first read, I thought I'd misread it.

sc084.text: Wu and Shu sent relief; Sima Yi had officers block them.

sc085.text: In 16 days the city fell, and Meng Da was killed.

sc086.text: Then he marched back to Wancheng.

sc087.text: He went to court once; the emperor sent him back to Wancheng.

sc088.text: Remember the opening? On the day of the Empty Fort, where was Sima Yi?

sc089.text: The records put two things in the same month: in the first month of 228, Xincheng fell;

sc091.text: That spring, he spread word he'd take another road, but led his main force to attack Qishan.

sc093.text: Grand General Cao Zhen held the west; Zhang He was sent to fight at Jieting.

sc094.text: Even Emperor Ming of Wei came to Chang'an.

sc095.text: Sima Yi is not on this list.

sc096.text: Look again: he's just not there.

sc097.text: In the novel, Sima Zhao too advises his father at the walls; he was about 18, and the histories don't say he went.

sc098.text: Ma Su led Shu at Jieting.

sc099.text: Ignoring Zhuge Liang's plan, he left water for the hill.

sc100.text: Wang Ping kept warning. No use.

sc101.text: No water. How long could they hold?

sc102.text: Zhang He arrived and cut the path to the hill's water.

sc106.text: Leading them: Wang Ping, who had just warned Ma Su.

sc108.text: Say you're Zhang He: fresh from a big win, yet below, a unit won't flee or scatter, drums still beating. Dare you chase?

sc109.text: Zhang He halted; suspecting an ambush, he held back.

sc110.text: Remember the man at the hill's foot who kept drumming? It was Wang Ping; the one fooled: Zhang He.

sc111.text: And so Wang Ping slowly gathered the scattered men and led them back.

sc114.text: He was sent to Jingzhou, under Sima Yi.

sc115.text: What was Sima Yi doing that winter? Building a navy in Jingzhou to hit Wu by river.

sc116.text: Winter shallows stalled ships; Zhang He withdrew to Fangcheng.

sc117.text: So when did Sima Yi really head west?

sc118.text: Two years later. The Xicheng Pei Songzhi mentioned comes in now.

sc119.text: In 230 Sima Yi really set out from Xicheng, cutting mountain roads to attack Hanzhong.

sc120.text: If you love place names, watch out here.

sc121.text: That Xicheng is on the upper Han River, not the novel's Xicheng County.

sc122.text: Zhuge Liang waited for Wei at Chiban, Chenggu.

sc123.text: Over 30 days of rain cut the plank roads; Wei withdrew.

sc125.text: Pei Songzhi said someone had to die before they'd meet. Who?

sc126.text: It was Cao Zhen. In 231, Cao Zhen fell gravely ill.

sc127.text: The emperor told Sima Yi: the west matters too much; only you can be trusted with it.

sc128.text: With Cao Zhen dead, Sima Yi was sent west from Jingzhou.

sc129.text: Zhuge Liang besieged Qishan; Sima Yi attacked.

sc130.text: It was the two men's first real clash.

sc131.text: Back to that question: did Zhuge Liang ever really bluff Sima Yi into retreat?

sc132.text: Once. Three years later, Zhuge Liang died of illness in camp.

sc133.text: After Zhuge Liang died, Shu turned banners and beat drums as if to charge Sima Yi.

sc134.text: Yet Sima Yi retreated, not daring to press.

sc135.text: People coined a saying: a dead Zhuge put a living Zhongda to flight. Zhongda was Sima Yi.

sc136.text: Sima Yi said: I can foresee the living, not the dead.

sc137.text: I think that line's kind of cute.

sc138.text: He wasn't on the list we just saw. Whatever Guo Chong or the novel says, Zhuge Liang's real foe that year wasn't Sima Yi.

sc139.text: We think that year's real bluff wasn't the tower's zither, but the drum below Jieting's hill.

sc142.text: Novel, stage or TV: where'd you first see the Empty Fort? Tell me.

sc143.text: This channel covers only what's on record. Subscribe to open files with us.
